name: Ventoy
for: Put many ISOs on one stick — no re-flashing. Works for Linux and Windows.
install: Set the stick up once, then it's drag-and-drop forever after.
Windows: download the Ventoy .zip, extract it, and run Ventoy2Disk.exe.
Pick your USB in the Device dropdown, then click Install. This wipes the whole stick — confirm the two warnings.

Linux: download the .tar.gz, extract it, open a terminal in that folder, and run the install command below (or use the web GUI: sudo sh VentoyWeb.sh, then open the localhost link it prints and click Install).
code:
# Linux — one-time setup (replace sdX with your USB from lsblk)
sudo sh Ventoy2Disk.sh -i /dev/sdX
use: That's the hard part done. From now on you never flash again.
Just copy any .iso file onto the Ventoy drive — drag-and-drop in your file manager, or cp on Linux.
Add as many ISOs as fit — mix Linux distros and Windows freely.
Boot the PC from the USB. Ventoy shows a menu of every ISO on the stick; pick one and it boots.
tips: The Install step happens once. After that, adding a new distro is literally copying a file.
Secure Boot: Ventoy supports it, but if a distro refuses to boot, disable Secure Boot in the BIOS or switch Ventoy to GRUB2 mode.
Leave the stick on the default exFAT/FAT32 so both Windows and Linux ISOs work.

name: Rufus
for: The go-to for Windows ISOs (and single Linux ISOs) on a Windows PC.
install: Rufus is a single portable .exe — nothing to install.
Download it and double-click to run.
use: Plug in the USB. Rufus auto-selects it under Device — double-check it's the right one, because it gets wiped.
Click SELECT and choose your .iso file.
Leave Partition scheme on the auto-detected value (GPT for modern UEFI machines).
Windows 11 only: Rufus pops a dialog — tick 'Remove requirement for 4GB+ RAM, Secure Boot and TPM 2.0' and 'Remove requirement for an online Microsoft account' if you want those bypasses.
Click START, then confirm the 'all data will be destroyed' warning.
Wait for the green READY bar, then close Rufus and eject the stick.
tips: Rufus automatically splits the oversized Windows install file that a plain FAT32 stick can't hold — that's why it's the tool for Windows USBs.
GPT vs MBR: choose GPT + UEFI for anything made in the last ~10 years.
If a Linux ISO won't boot, redo it and pick 'DD Image' mode when Rufus asks, instead of ISO mode.

name: balenaEtcher
for: The simplest cross-platform way to flash a single ISO. Hard to get wrong.
install: Download the installer for your OS and run it.
On Linux it's an AppImage — make it executable (chmod +x) and double-click.
use: Select target — choose your USB. Etcher hides your system drives, so you can't wipe your OS by accident.
Flash! — enter your password and wait. Etcher verifies the write automatically when it's done.
tips: Genuinely the friendliest option — great for a first-timer.
One ISO per stick: re-flashing replaces whatever was on it (unlike Ventoy).
AppImage won't open on Linux? Run chmod +x balenaEtcher*.AppImage, or install the libfuse2 package.

name: dd (command line)
for: Linux/macOS users who want zero extra software. Powerful and unforgiving.
install: Nothing to install — dd is already on every Linux and macOS system.
code:
lsblk                              # find your USB, e.g. /dev/sdb (the disk, not sdb1)
sudo umount /dev/sdX*              # unmount it (don't physically eject)
sudo dd if=/path/to/distro.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress oflag=sync
sync
use: Plug in the USB and find its device name: lsblk on Linux, or diskutil list on macOS. It's the whole disk (like /dev/sdb), not a partition (no number on the end).
Unmount it — but don't eject it.
Run the dd command, pointing if= at your ISO and of= at the USB disk.
Wait for it to finish (status=progress shows how far along it is), then run sync to be sure it's fully written.
warn: dd has no undo and asks for no confirmation. If you put the wrong device in of=, it overwrites that disk instantly — including your main drive. Always run lsblk first and read the device name twice.
tips: bs=4M makes it fast; oflag=sync makes sure everything is written before the command returns.
On macOS use /dev/rdiskN (the raw device) and bs=4m for a big speed-up.
